articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Amalthea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
articles.text:
On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Amalthea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be a last of its kind.
On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists.
The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft.
The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong. However, NASA quickly fixed the problem and got Galileo working again.
Less than a year later, Galileo threw itself into Jupiter's atmosphere. The spacecraft was crushed by the high pressure in Jupiter's atmosphere, but its data still survives on Earth.
Why it mattered
The Galileo spacecraft was running on cosmic fumes by the time it reached Amalthea and the flyby would be the last time the probe would ever swing by one of Jupiter's moons.
While it may not look like it in Galileo's black and white images above and below, Amalthea is tinted red due sulfur contamination on its surface. The moon is small, about 168 miles long, and orbits about 112,468 miles (181,000 km) from Jupiter (much closer to the planet than the Earth and its moon).
Galileo flew within 99 miles of Amalthea during its flyby, which also marked the closest Galileo would get to Jupiter before its death dive in September 2005.
"Scientists studying data from NASA's Galileo spacecraft have found that Jupiter's moon Amalthea is a pile of icy rubble less dense than water," NASA announced in May 2005
"Amalthea is throwing us a curve ball," Torrence Johnson, a study co-author on the Almathea flyby and project scientist for the Galileo mission at JPL, said in 2005. "Its density is well below that of water ice, and even with substantial porosity, Amalthea probably contains a lot of water ice, as well as rock."
Originally known as Jupiter V (because it was the fifth Jupiter moon discovered after the so-called Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto), Amalthea was named after naiad, or water nymph, from Greek mythology.
It is fitting that Amalthea was the last of Jupiter's moons to be visited by the Galileo spacecraft. The moon was also last Jupiter moon to be discovered by visual observations when it was first disovered by astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard in September 1892 using the Lick Observatory telescope in California.
The Galileo spacecraft ultimately crashed into Jupiter on Sept. 21, 2005, less than a year after its Amalthea flyby.
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.
Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.
- Tariq Malik Editor-in-Chief

articles.title: Trong 5 lời tiên tri của người Maya, 4 đã ứng nghiệm, tại sao chỉ có ngày tận thế là vô hiệu?
articles.text:
Trong thời cổ đại luôn có rất nhiều nhà tiên tri, và một số lời tiên tri đã thực sự chính xác một cách đáng kinh ngạc. Ví dụ, "Thôi Bối Đồ" do Lý Thuần Phong và Viên Thiên Cang thực hiện vào thời nhà Đường ở Trung Quốc đã dự đoán hướng đi của nhà Đường trong hàng nghìn năm. Điều quan trọng là một số điều ông dự đoán đã trở thành sự thật, chẳng hạn như sự ra đời của nhà Minh.
Nhưng thế giới đã thực sự bị sốc với những lời tiên tri của người Maya. Bạn nên biết nền văn minh Maya cách đây hàng ngàn năm đã rất phát triển trong nhiều lĩnh vực: văn học, toán học, thiên văn học, kiến trúc… Trong khi bốn lời tiên tri đầu tiên họ đưa ra đã ứng nghiệm, thì lời tiên tri cuối cùng là về ngày tận thế năm 2012, rất may chưa xảy ra. Vậy tại sao lời tiên tri thứ năm của người Maya lại không có giá trị?
Người Maya cho rằng tất cả mọi thứ trên thế giới đều phát triển thường xuyên và theo chu kỳ. (Ảnh minh họa).
Nền văn minh Maya có lẽ tồn tại từ thế kỷ thứ 10 trước Công nguyên đến giữa và cuối thế kỷ thứ 8 sau Công nguyên, là một tộc người rất cổ xưa và khôn ngoan, được đặt theo tên của người Maya thuộc Ấn Độ. Nền văn minh này được khai sinh độc lập bởi người da đỏ Maya, tách biệt với các nền văn minh cổ đại của châu Á, châu Phi và châu Âu, là nền văn minh cổ đại duy nhất trên thế giới được sinh ra trong rừng rậm nhiệt đới thay vì lưu vực sông. Những lời tiên tri mà người Maya để lại đề cập đến tổng cộng năm chu kỳ hủy diệt và tái sinh trong thế giới của chúng ta.
Một chu kỳ được gọi là Thời đại Mặt trời. Thời đại Mặt trời đầu tiên trong các thời đại Mặt trời trước đó là nền văn minh Gendaya. Nền văn minh này được phóng đại hơn. Nó được cho là một nền văn minh siêu sức mạnh. Nhưng có rất ít thông tin về nó, vì vậy không có cơ sở lý thuyết hiện đại. Thời đại mặt trời thứ hai cũng là nền văn minh Lưỡng Hà, là sự tiếp nối của nền văn minh trước đó, nhưng trong thời đại mặt trời này, các siêu cường đã biến mất.
Thời đại mặt trời thứ ba là nền văn minh Murian, đây cũng là sự tiếp nối của nền văn minh trước, họ bắt đầu sử dụng năng lượng thực vật. Nền văn minh này đã bị phá hủy bởi sự chìm của lục địa, và thời đại mặt trời thứ tư là nền văn minh Atlantis quen thuộc hơn. Họ kế thừa nền văn minh cuối cùng, không phải sự tiếp nối, bởi vì Atlantis đến từ những người thuộc địa của Orion. Nó đã tồn tại từ thời của nền văn minh Murian, và đã có những cuộc chiến tranh giữa hai nền văn minh này, và nó cũng đã bị phá hủy bởi thiên tai. Năm cuối cùng, 2012, sẽ là bắt đầu của kỷ nguyên mặt trời thứ năm, một năm mà sự sống ở Bắc bán cầu sẽ chết và nền văn minh sẽ tan rã.
Bốn kỷ nguyên mặt trời đầu tiên không thể được xác nhận vì thiếu dữ liệu, và người Maya không chỉ đưa ra dự đoán về kỷ nguyên mặt trời. Có bốn lời tiên tri khác, lời tiên đoán đầu tiên dự đoán sự xuất hiện của ô tô và máy bay trên thế giới, thứ hai tiên đoán Thế chiến thứ hai, thứ ba tiên đoán sự ra đời của Hitler và thứ tư dự đoán sự kết thúc của chính người Maya. Cái cuối cùng là ngày tận thế ngày 20 tháng 12 năm 2012. Không khó để chúng ta trong xã hội hiện đại nhận thấy rằng 4 cái đầu tiên đã được hiện thực hóa, và chúng cực kỳ chính xác vào thời điểm diễn ra Thế chiến và sự ra đời của Hitler. Vậy tại sao lời tiên tri về ngày tận thế cuối cùng lại không trở thành sự thật?
Sau khi nghiên cứu trong một thời gian dài, một số chuyên gia đã đưa ra một số suy đoán, liệu có phải chúng ta đã hiểu sai về dự đoán cuối cùng hay không. Lời tiên tri thực sự đề cập đến sự thay thế của các nền văn minh. Người Maya cảm thấy rằng tất cả mọi thứ trên thế giới đều phát triển thường xuyên và theo chu kỳ. Và sau thế kỷ 21, loài người đã đi một con đường hoàn toàn khác với xã hội trước đây, chẳng phải giống như một sự thay thế của nền văn minh sao?
Người Maya cũng đã từng nói, Trái đất không phải là sở hữu của nhân loại, mà nhân loại thuộc về Trái đất. Hiện nay chúng ta đang sinh sống ở kỷ nguyên mặt trời thứ 5. Do đó, người Maya nói ngày 20 tháng 12 năm 2012 kết thúc, không phải là là ngày tận thế, mà là thời điểm tinh thần của con người bắt đầu thức tỉnh và phát triển nhanh chóng, nhận thức của con người đối với vũ trụ sẽ đạt đết trình độ cao hơn.

articles.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
articles.text:
A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- ALMA
- Summary:
- Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.
- Share:
Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.
Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.
The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.
Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.
"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."
Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming
The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.
At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.
The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).
Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer
The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.
Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.
This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."
A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse
One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.
The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."
Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.
"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.
As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.
In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.
Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues
The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.
To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.
They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.
This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.
The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.
Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse
Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.
More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.
Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.
The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."
Journal Reference:
- L. D. Matthews, A. K. Dupree, A. M. S. Richards, W. R. F. Dent. New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion. The Astronomical Journal, 2026; 172 (3): 184 DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae953d

articles.title: You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters
articles.text:
You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters
After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.
TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? 
For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection.
Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it.
"The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said. "It's to do something that only 651 people have been able to do: miss Earth and miss other Earthlings."
Glover was one of the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. Alongside NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them.
As the Orion spacecraft traversed the far side of the moon, the Artemis II crew watched Earth disappear below the lunar horizon before losing radio contact with our planet. Around 40 minutes later, Earth came back into view as the spacecraft emerged from behind the moon.
For Glover, however, the experience was about much more than the view. He believes that if everyone on Earth had the opportunity to make the same journey, they would come away with a similar appreciation for what they'd left behind.
"I think all of us would say something in our native language, in the most basic way we can communicate about love, joy, hope and inspiration," Glover said.
Although Glover shared the extraordinary journey with three fellow astronauts, the four of them were separated from the rest of humanity by hundreds of thousands of miles.
And for Glover, that distance brought with it a strange contradiction: the farther he traveled from humanity, the more he longed to connect with it.
"At the point of ultimate disconnection, [there is] this longing for connection," Glover said.
The experience gave him a perspective that he carried back into everyday life.
"There are moments where I am rushing through traffic and want to get where I'm going because I'm being selfish," Glover admitted. "But I don't have to stay there."
Instead, he remembers what it felt like to look back at a planet so distant that everyone who has ever lived could be covered by his hand.
"I wish you could all feel what it's like to come back home after that disconnection," he said.
The 'sea level effect'
Astronauts often describe experiencing the "overview effect", a profound shift in perspective that can come from seeing Earth from space. But Glover believes that there's something equally powerful waiting to be discovered much closer to home.
When asked by a Starmus VIII attendee whether people needed to undergo something extraordinary to develop a greater sense of kindness toward others, his answer was no.
Glover encouraged people to look more closely at the natural world around them, whether that meant walking along the beach, watching the ocean or simply examining a leaf held up to sunlight. 
Even something as ordinary as a leaf, he explained, is capable of turning sunlight into food through photosynthesis. And although science can explain how that happens, understanding the process doesn't make it any less remarkable.
"We have to choose to be moved by these things," Glover said.
He worries that modern life, with its endless technological distractions, has made it all too easy to overlook the extraordinary things happening around us.
"Familiarity breeds contempt. Have you heard this? I think it's worse than that. Familiarity breeds indifference," he said.
Glover has a name for this perspective he hopes people can rediscover without traveling into space: The sea level effect.
It's about finding the same sense of wonder and connection that astronauts experience in orbit, but right here on Earth, where most of us spend our lives. And ultimately, Glover believes the greatest wonder isn't the moon, the stars, or even the incredible complexity of nature. It's the people we share our planet with.
"I think the hardest place to see this miracle is in the actual greatest miracle in the universe: other humans," he said.
"We all feel it with babies, but when we get old enough to have opinions, we start to want to argue with each other."
Glover hopes that by taking the time to appreciate the natural world, people might become a little more willing to appreciate one another too.
"That's the mission that I want to be part of for the rest of my life," Glover said.
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

articles.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
articles.text:
Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- Keck School of Medicine of USC
- Summary:
- A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.
- Share:
Children who consume more ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may have stronger brain responses to tempting foods, potentially helping explain why these products are associated with weight gain. A new study published in JAMA Network Open found that children who ate more of these foods showed heightened activity in the brain's reward system when looking at pictures of appetizing foods. Those stronger responses were also associated with increases in body fat over the following year.
Ultra-processed foods include many everyday products, such as breakfast cereals, packaged bread, and instant soups. They are manufactured to be appealing, convenient, and able to remain fresh for extended periods. Many contain artificial sweeteners, coloring agents, and other ingredients rarely used in home cooking. These products make up a substantial portion of children's diets, accounting for approximately 67% of the calories consumed by children in the United States.
Previous research has associated ultra-processed food consumption with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. However, scientists are still trying to understand the biological processes that might explain these connections. The new investigation, supported in part by the National Institutes of Health, combined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), dietary assessments, and measurements of children's body composition to explore whether the brain's response to food could play a role.
"Children's brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It's an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment," said the study's senior author, Kathleen A. Page, MD, professor of medicine and pediatrics and co-chief of the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. "We're particularly interested in understanding these processes in children, because we believe that intervening early could make a real difference."
Brain Scans Reveal a Link to Future Weight Gain
To investigate these connections, the research team studied 46 children between the ages of seven and 10 who were enrolled in the ongoing BrainChild study, which examines factors contributing to diabetes and obesity. Every participant had a healthy weight when the research began, giving scientists an opportunity to investigate potential warning signs before excess weight developed.
At the start of the study, the children underwent brain scans while looking at pictures of appealing foods (such as cookies or French fries). Researchers also gathered information about their diets and recorded several health measurements, including body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and waist circumference. After one year, the team measured these physical characteristics again to identify changes.
The brain scans revealed a notable pattern. Children who consumed larger amounts of ultra-processed foods showed greater activity in the dorsal striatum when viewing food pictures. This part of the brain helps regulate reward and motivation, making it particularly relevant to how people respond to desirable foods.
Importantly, children with stronger responses in this brain region also tended to experience greater increases in BMI and body fat percentage over the next year. The findings suggest that heightened sensitivity to food cues may be one factor connecting ultra-processed diets with subsequent weight gain.
How Brain Reward Activity May Influence Body Fat
By the end of the study, children who consumed more ultra-processed foods generally had higher BMI, greater body fat percentage, and larger waist circumference.
The researchers then examined whether differences in brain activity could help account for these associations. When they adjusted their analysis to consider the children's responses in the dorsal striatum, the relationship between ultra-processed food intake and BMI became 31% weaker. The corresponding association with body fat percentage decreased by 44%.
These reductions suggest that the brain's reward response may help explain part of the relationship between ultra-processed food consumption and changes in body composition. Although the results do not demonstrate that these foods directly alter brain function, they provide a possible biological explanation for an association that has been observed in previous research.
"This study goes beyond just understanding that UPFs affect weight gain," Page said. "It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time."
Making Healthier Foods More Accessible
The researchers caution that improving children's diets cannot depend entirely on individual families. Ultra-processed products are often inexpensive, widely available, and easy to prepare, making them practical choices for households facing financial or time constraints.
"Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution," Page said.
There are also important limitations to consider. Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether eating ultra-processed foods directly causes heightened brain activity or increases in body weight. The findings establish relationships between these factors, but additional research is needed to determine whether one causes another.
Page hopes to address that question in a future intervention study. The proposed research would provide children who regularly consume ultra-processed foods with more minimally processed alternatives. Scientists could then examine whether changing their diets affects how their brains respond to food images and whether any differences are associated with reduced weight gain.
Meanwhile, the BrainChild study will continue tracking participants as they move through puberty and into early adulthood. By monitoring brain development, body composition, dietary patterns, and general health over time, researchers hope to gain a clearer picture of how childhood nutrition may influence long-term health.
Research Team and Funding
The study was led by Page alongside Jasmin M. Alves, Ella Morgan, Brendan Angelo, Kianna Le, and Jared Smith from the Division of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine, and Diabetes and Obesity Research Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California. Additional contributors included Kay Jann of the USC Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, University of Southern California, and Ting Chow and Anny H. Xiang of the Department of Research and Evaluation at Kaiser Permanente Southern California in Pasadena, California.
Funding came from an American Diabetes Association Pathway Accelerator Award [1-14-ACE-36] and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) [R01DK116858, R01DK134079]. Support for the REDCap database used in the research was provided by the Southern California Clinical and Translational Science Institute [NIH UL1TR001855].

articles.title: Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội: Công bố ca song thai cùng trứng cực kỳ đặc biệt, thế giới mới ghi nhận 1 trường hợp
articles.text:
Đây là lần đầu tiên tại Việt Nam phát hiện ca song thai đặc biệt như vậy và là ca thứ 2 trên thế giới.
Y văn ghi nhận mang thai đôi cùng trứng xuất hiện khi trứng sau khi được thụ tinh thì phân chia thành hai phôi và từ đó phát triển thành hai cá thể riêng rẽ. Quá trình này hình thành ngay từ giai đoạn đầu tiên, khi phôi thai chỉ là một chùm tế bào. Trẻ sinh đôi cùng trứng sẽ giống nhau hoàn toàn về hình thức, giới tính.
Tuy nhiên với trường hợp vừa được Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội công bố là trường hợp đặc biệt hiếm trên thế giới.
Đây là trường hợp cực hiếm, lần đầu tiên được Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội phát hiện. (Ảnh minh họa).
Thai phụ 23 tuổi, mang thai lần đầu tự nhiên. Kết quả siêu âm cho thấy chung một bánh rau, hai buồng ối từ tuần thai thứ 8. Thai phụ đến Đơn vị Can thiệp bào thai, Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà nội thăm khám ở tuần thai 16 vì có 1 thai phù.
Sau khi hội chẩn, siêu âm và chọc ối phát hiện thai A phù thai, giới tính nữ, kiểu gene nữ Turner(45,X). Thai B bình thường về mặt hình thái và giới tính trên siêu âm là nam, kiểu gene nam (46,XY). Các xét nghiệm di truyền chuyên sâu khác cũng đã được thực hiện và chứng minh rằng 2 thai này chung 1 trứng nhưng có kiểu gene khác nhau.
PGS.TS Nguyễn Duy Ánh, Giám đốc Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội, cho biết đây là trường hợp cực hiếm, lần đầu tiên được Bệnh viện phát hiện.
Bác sĩ TS. Nguyễn Thị Sim, người trực tiếp thực hiện các xét nghiệm phát hiện ra song thai bất thường cho biết: “Các chứng minh của Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội cho thấy vẫn có một số trẻ song thai cùng trứng không giống nhau 100% về kiểu gene và kiểu hình. Với năng lực chẩn đoán toàn diện cùng đầy đủ trang thiết bị hiện đại cần thiết, Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội thực hiện khám, siêu âm và xét nghiệm di truyền chuyên sâu phát hiện nhiều ca bệnh hiếm gặp. Ca bệnh hi hữu đặc biệt này đã cung cấp một góc nhìn hoàn toàn mới, sâu và rộng hơn cho ngành Di truyền học và ngành Sản phụ khoa”.
Được biết ca bệnh được hội chẩn tư vấn kĩ, chỉ định các xét nghiệm di truyền chuyên sâu hiện đại ngay từ trong bụng mẹ ra được kết quả bất thường trước sinh. Từ ca bệnh này cho thấy khi có những ca bất thường cần xét nghiệm di truyền.
TS Nguyễn Duy Ánh cho biết từ ca bệnh này cho thấy khi có những ca bất thường cần xét nghiệm di truyền. “Phát hiện này của bác sĩ Bệnh viện Phụ sản Hà Nội cho thấy không phải cứ sinh đôi cùng trứng là giống nhau để rồi bỏ qua những ca bệnh hiếm, những bất thường về mặt di truyền”, TS Ánh nói.
Do thai bị khiếm khuyết về mặt di truyền cùng khả năng duy trì thai khó nên gia đình đã xin đình chỉ thai nghén. Đáng chú ý, ở thai nam do bất thường về gene nên sẽ không có khả năng sinh sản nếu được chào đời và trưởng thành.
“Về nguyên nhân dẫn đến bất thường rất khó. Chúng ta có thể loại trừ nguyên nhân có sẵn từ bố mẹ. Đây là những trường hợp đột biến mới phát sinh. Đây là trường hợp hiếm của hiếm khi kết hợp nhiều bất thường về di truyền”, TS Trần Đức Phấn, Chủ tịch Hội Di truyền học Việt Nam cho biết.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 probe bounces back from communications glitch in interstellar space
articles.text:
NASA's Voyager 1 probe bounces back from communications glitch in interstellar space
"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this."
Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month.
The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix.
"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.
Voyager 1 is almost one light-day from Earth, meaning that a command takes nearly a day to reach the spacecraft and a response takes another day to come back to our planet. The spacecraft will reach the light-day milestone on Nov. 18, at 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth.
NASA's Deep Space Network of three antennas does check-ins to make sure the spacecraft is doing well. On Oct. 18 and 19, Voyager 1 did not respond. Its signal fortunately reappeared on Oct. 20.
"Engineers still are investigating what caused the communication loss," JPL added in the statement, but said it appears Voyager 1 went into a sort of safe mode. "The team has so far determined that one group of thrusters went offline and their backups turned on. Such a swap is programmed to occur automatically if the spacecraft computers detect something amiss with the active thrusters."
Voyager 1 and its still-operational twin, Voyager 2, both launched in 1977 on an initial mission to explore planets in the solar system. The two spacecraft took advantage of a rare alignment that allowed them to swing from Jupiter to Saturn to Uranus and Neptune using a minimum of fuel, although funding to explore the more distant planets and moons was not guaranteed at launch.
The spacecraft duly swung by Jupiter's and Saturn's systems (some months apart from each other) to great acclaim before parting pathways. Voyager 1's close-up view of Saturn's rings as well as the moon Titan — which may have prebiotic or pre-life chemistry — altered the spacecraft's trajectory to put it high above the plane of the solar system. Meanwhile, Voyager 2 flew on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively, providing the only up-close view of these planetary systems to date.
Running on nuclear power, and continuing to deliver valuable science from deep space, the Voyagers saw their missions extended repeatedly. Both crossed into interstellar space a few years ago, and are still operational.
But with age comes a cost: the plutonium power sources on both spacecraft are diminishing, requiring engineers to periodically shut off instruments or come up with other clever ways of saving power. Voyager 1 just underwent one of those power adjustments, nicknamed the "Big Bang" because it reconfigured a number of spacecraft instruments.
"In early September, engineers successfully turned off three devices on the Voyager 1 spacecraft and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives," JPL wrote of the effort, noting that Voyager 2 also had a "Big Bang" about six weeks previous to that.
JPL did not provide an estimate for how long the missions could keep running, but noted each spacecraft loses four watts of power a year — each launched with 470 watts — and that the spacecraft could continue operating science instruments "longer than previously anticipated" due to the Big Bang. On Voyager 1, for example, the falling power would have otherwise meant switching off another instrument possibly as soon as next summer.
In 2022, Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, stated the hope was the mission would continue to operate into the 2030s.
Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

articles.title: Người Đông Á mang gene một loài người khác với nhiều bất thường
articles.text:
Nhóm nghiên cứu từ Anh đã tìm ra câu trả lời cho bí ẩn hóc búa: Loài người cổ Neanderthals sinh sống chủ yếu ở châu Âu, vì sao người Đông Á lại mang DNA của họ nhiều nhất thế giới?
Nghiên cứu dẫn đầu bởi nhà sinh thái và tiến hóa Claudio Quilodrán từ Đại học Oxford (Anh), cho thấy lịch sử di cư và tiến hóa của nhân loại có thể cần được viết lại.
Người Neanderthals khác loài nhưng cùng thuộc chi Homo (chi Người) với Homo sapiens chúng ta. Họ từng hôn phối dị chủng với các cộng đồng Homo sapiens di cư từ châu Phi tới, do đó hầu như tất cả những người bên ngoài châu Phi ngày nay đều có một ít Neanderthals trong dòng máu - trung bình 2% bộ gene.
Tất cả chúng ta đều có một ít Neanderthals trong dòng máu - (Ảnh đồ họa: Joe McNally)
Người châu Âu, đặc biệt là người Bắc Âu, mang khá nhiền DNA Neanderthals, vì khu vực này là nơi sinh sống chủ yếu của loài người cổ này. Nhưng gần đây, các nhà nghiên cứu phát hiện ra điều vô lý: Người gốc Đông Á có nhiều gene Neanderthals hơn người châu Âu từ 8-24%.
Theo Live Science, tiến sĩ Quilodrán và các cộng sự phát hiện ra rằng một làn sóng nông dân di cư từ Trung Đông cổ đại có thể giải thích điều tưởng chừng như "ngược đời nói trên".
Bài công bố trên tạp chí Science Advances đưa ra một đoạn lịch sử cổ đại phức tạp hơn rất nhiều những gì giới khoa học biết đến trước đây.
Đầu tiên, từ khoảng 60.000-70.000 năm trước làn sóng Homo sapiens di cư từ châu Phi đến phần thế giới còn lại và là tổ tiên của nhóm "người lai" Homo sapiens - Neanderthals đầu tiên.
Người Neanderthals có thể sinh sống phổ biến hơn ở châu Âu, nhưng cũng ở các nơi khác. Người Homo sapiens thì phân tán khắp các vùng đất họ có thể tìm đến.
Vì vậy, dòng máu Neanderthals được đưa vào người hiện đại ở khắp nơi, khiến họ không bao giờ biến mất hoàn toàn dù đã tuyệt chủng khoảng hơn 30.000 năm trước.
Tuy nhiên, một làn sóng di cư khác từ châu Phi vào 10.000 năm trước đến cùng châu Âu đã làm thay đổi cục diện. Họ cũng lai Neanderthals, nhưng đậm đặc Homo sapiens hơn và là nhóm mang yếu tố Neanderthals ít nhất thế giới.
Họ là những người nông dân mà tổ tiên đã chọn Trung Đông và Tây Nam Á để định cư lại vào thời điểm Homo sapiens bắt đầu rời châu Phi.
Chính dòng máu ít yếu tố Neanderthals này đã pha loãng các yếu tố Neanderthals trong bộ gene của người châu Âu.
Kết quả này được đúc kết từ quá trình xem xét hơn 4.400 bộ gene của người Homo sapiens, từ 40.000 năm trước đến hiện đại, đã được giải trình tự trước đây.
Tỉ lệ DNA của người Neanderthals trong bộ gene đã tiết lộ chi tiết về cách các nhóm người thuộc các loài khác nhau di cư và hôn phối dị chủng với nhau.
Hiểu được sâu sắc hơn về "dòng máu lai" trong mỗi chúng ta có ý nghĩa rất lớn trong việc hiểu được cách mà nhân loại đã tiến hóa, cũng như tác động đến một số nghiên cứu về y học, vì các gene khác loài thường mang đến nhiều đặc điểm riêng biệt, làm tăng hay giảm nguy cơ một số bệnh tật.

articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
articles.text:
The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.
- Share:
The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.
In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.
"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."
How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear
To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.
The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.
At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.
"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.
Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger
Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.
The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.
Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.
"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."
The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.
A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD
The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.
For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.
The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.
"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."
Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.
Study Details and Funding
The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.
The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

articles.title: Qua bẫy ảnh phát hiện một số loài động vật quý hiếm ở Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên
articles.text:
Thông qua bẫy ảnh, Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên đã phát hiện một số loài động vật cực kỳ nguy cấp như gà lôi tía; một số loài nguy cấp, sắp nguy cấp như: cầy vằn bắc, cầy vòi mốc, gà so núi.
Theo thông tin của Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên, thực hiện Chương trình “Điều tra, đánh giá các loài thú tại Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên”, từ tháng 4 - 10/2024, Trung tâm Du lịch và Bảo tồn sinh vật Hoàng Liên (Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên) đã thực hiện lắp đặt 20 máy bẫy ảnh trên 3 tuyến điều tra.
Cán bộ Trung tâm du lịch và bảo tồn sinh vật Hoàng Liên (Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên)  thực hiện đặt bẫy ảnh tại tuyến điều tra. (Ảnh: Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên).
Các điểm bẫy ảnh được thiết lập theo ô lưới ngoài hiện trường ở sinh cảnh rừng chủ yếu các loài cây dẻ, sồi, vối thuốc,… mọc xen lẫn với các loài cây vầu, trúc, sặt, các loài cây bụi thảm tươi như cỏ gianh, ràng ràng, dương xỉ, cói.
Hình ảnh Gà lôi tía (Tragopan temminckii (Gray, 1831). (Ảnh: Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên).
Các điểm bẫy ảnh cách nhau khoảng 500m và được gắn chặt vào các thân cây ở chiều cao từ 20 đến 40cm so với mặt đất, nhằm tối đa hóa khả năng ghi nhận loài mục tiêu của nghiên cứu.
Hình ảnh Cầy vòi mốc (Paguma larvata). (Ảnh: Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên).
Kết quả thu được trên tuy chưa thể hiện hết hình ảnh đa dạng các loài động vật tại Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên (Lào Cai) nhưng phần nào cho thấy sự xuất hiện một số loài động vật hiếm gặp tại đây, chứng tỏ công tác quản lý bảo vệ rừng đã và đang thực hiện tốt.
Hình ảnh Gà so núi (Bambusicola  spp). (Ảnh: Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên).
Với kết quả lần đầu tiên được thực hiện cho thấy Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên đang sở hữu tài nguyên đa dạng sinh học phong phú, độc đáo, có tiềm năng du lịch sinh thái, cần được tăng cường bảo vệ và giám sát đa dạng sinh học.
Hình ảnh Cầy vằn bắc (Chrotogale owstoni). (Ảnh: Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên).
Kế hoạch trong thời gian tới, Trung tâm Du lịch và Bảo tồn sinh vật Hoàng Liên trực thuộc Vườn quốc gia Hoàng Liên sẽ phối hợp với các đơn vị tiếp tục lắp đặt máy bẫy ảnh ở nhiều sinh cảnh khác nhau nhằm điều tra, đánh giá một số loài thú cụ thể tại vườn quốc gia này.

articles.title: Earth photobombs spacewalking Canadian astronaut | Space photo of the day for Nov. 5, 2026
articles.text:
Earth photobombs spacewalking Canadian astronaut | Space photo of the day for Nov. 5, 2026
What a view.
Spacewalks are hard work, so sometimes you need to take a break for a moment and snap a gorgeous selfie with your home planet in the background.
What is it?
During a pre-Halloween spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk took a moment to pose for a photograph.
In this moment, the International Space Station to which he was tethered was orbiting 267 miles (430 kilometers) above the South Atlantic Ocean down below on Earth.
During this spacewalk — the first for a Canadian since 2019 — Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon worked together to install a new roll-out solar array on the station while also performing some "get ahead" tasks to prep for the next spacewalk, which is happening today (Nov. 5).
During today's excursion, the same two astronauts will venture out into space, tethered to the space station, to install the eighth and final roll-out solar array. These eight new arrays will boost the station's available power by a total of 30%, according to NASA officials.
Why is it incredible?
When we think of astronauts working in space, we might think of the important science and research they're doing aboard the station. Astronauts work on everything from biomedical research to plant science and physics experiments. But the job also includes work on the space station itself.
Sometimes they have to venture out into the vacuum of space to fix urgent problems. These situations can be tense, and there's a lot of pressure to get things absolutely right.
But even spacewalks that do relatively mundane maintenance work, like the one on Oct. 29, come with pressure. Every minute that astronauts spend outside of the space station, there are countless risk factors floating around. Earth orbit is a very harsh environment, after all, even if it does allow for some pretty amazing selfies.
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

articles.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
articles.text:
A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- Smithsonian
- Summary:
- A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.
- Share:
For nearly 50 years, scientists have struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's richest regions for amphibian diversity. Beginning in the 1970s, researchers documented dramatic population declines, but the cause of these losses remained uncertain.
Now, scientists have uncovered compelling evidence pointing to a deadly fungal disease as the likely explanation. The findings, published in Molecular Ecology, come from researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU).
The suspected culprit is chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, a disease caused by the microscopic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s. However, the fungus was not formally identified and described until 1999, long after devastating amphibian declines had begun.
By then, hundreds of amphibian species worldwide had been driven toward extinction, and some had already disappeared. Because so many populations collapsed before scientists knew the fungus existed, determining whether it was responsible has been particularly difficult.
"After almost 50 years, we still aren't confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology," said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research.
A 50-Year-Old Mystery in Brazil's Atlantic Forest
One of these longstanding mysteries centers on the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, where amphibian populations experienced severe declines between 1979 and 1982.
Some researchers previously suggested that climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the disappearances. The new findings, however, provide evidence that an emerging fungal disease was spreading through the area at precisely the same time.
"While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances," Boyette said.
To investigate what happened, the researchers turned to an unexpected source of evidence: frogs preserved in museum collections decades earlier.
The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History houses specimens collected by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles. Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred.
These preserved animals offered scientists a rare opportunity to examine the period before and after the mysterious disappearances. By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread.
The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time.
Museum Specimens Reveal a Deadly Fungal Outbreak
The results revealed a striking change. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection. Among those collected during the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive for the fungus.
This sharp increase suggests that the pathogen arrived and spread through the local amphibian community around the same time that frog populations were collapsing.
But the researchers also uncovered a surprising pattern.
Species that suffered the most severe declines showed no detectable signs of infection in the preserved specimens. Meanwhile, species whose populations remained relatively stable frequently carried the fungus.
At first glance, these findings might seem to contradict the idea that chytrid caused the disappearances. The researchers believe the explanation may lie in differences in how individual species respond to the disease.
Some frogs may have been naturally capable of tolerating the infection, allowing them to survive even when the fungus was present. More vulnerable species, on the other hand, may have died so quickly after becoming infected that few or no infected individuals were ever collected.
"It's important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia," Boyette said. "The species that didn't decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them."
Together, the results suggest that chytrid spread rapidly among frogs with little previous exposure to the disease, with potentially devastating consequences for species unable to withstand infection.
Decades-Old Collections Help Solve a Wildlife Cold Case
For Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who contributed to the research, the findings demonstrate the extraordinary scientific value of natural history museums.
Specimens preserved many decades ago can contain biological evidence that researchers at the time had no way of recognizing. Modern testing methods now make it possible to revisit these collections and investigate outbreaks that occurred long before the responsible pathogens were discovered.
"Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery," Campana said.
Understanding these past outbreaks could also help scientists anticipate future threats.
One growing concern involves another fungal pathogen, B. salamandrivorans, which is threatening salamander populations in Europe and could pose a serious danger to salamanders in North America.
By reconstructing how earlier fungal diseases emerged, spread, and affected different species, researchers hope to improve their ability to recognize and respond to similar threats before they cause widespread damage.
Brazil's Frogs Show Surprising Signs of Recovery
Despite the devastating losses recorded decades ago, the latest findings also offer encouraging evidence of recovery.
Working with researchers from the University of São Paulo, the team made six visits to Boracéia between 2022 and 2024 to investigate the amphibians living there today.
Of the 17 species represented in Heyer's historical museum collection, researchers located 12 during their modern surveys. The remaining five were not found, leaving their current status uncertain and raising concerns that some may have disappeared from the site entirely.
Nevertheless, the surveys indicate that most amphibian species at Boracéia have recovered since the severe declines of the early 1980s.
The fungus has not disappeared. Chytrid infections are still present among local frogs, but the pattern of infection suggests that species once heavily affected by the disease may have developed greater tolerance over successive generations.
That increased tolerance could help explain why many populations have survived and rebounded despite continuing exposure to the pathogen.
The findings highlight an important distinction between infection and mortality. A species can carry a dangerous pathogen without necessarily suffering catastrophic losses, particularly if its members can tolerate the infection.
What the Discovery Means for Future Amphibian Survival
Although the evidence strongly implicates chytrid in the historic declines at Boracéia, the researchers caution that their findings apply to this particular location. The results cannot automatically explain amphibian disappearances elsewhere in the Atlantic Forest.
Still, the study provides a compelling explanation for a longstanding local mystery and demonstrates how scientists can use historical specimens to reconstruct outbreaks that would otherwise remain poorly understood.
The investigation is also continuing.
Researchers are now examining DNA recovered from museum specimens to identify the genetic mechanisms that influenced how amphibians responded to chytrid infections in the past. These analyses could help reveal why some species were devastated while others survived.
Separate projects are using ancient environmental DNA to help fill gaps in historical specimen records. This approach involves searching for genetic traces left behind by organisms in their surroundings, potentially providing evidence of species and pathogens that were never directly collected.
Together, these efforts could reveal a much clearer history of how chytrid emerged, spread, and affected amphibian biodiversity over the past century.
By uncovering the biological changes that helped some frogs survive and recover, scientists may also gain valuable insights into protecting vulnerable species from future fungal epidemics.

articles.title: Ai đã tạo ra gò rắn lớn nhất trên thế giới?
articles.text:
Ở miền đông Hoa Kỳ, nép mình giữa những tán cây bên cạnh một nhánh của sông Ohio là một trong những công trình kiến tạo kỳ lạ và bí ẩn nhất từng được tạo ra bởi con người. Great Serpent Mound hay còn gọi là gò rắn chỉ cao chưa đến 1 m, nhưng lại kéo dài hơn 400 mét và có thể nhìn thấy rõ ràng từ trên cao.
Gò đất đặc biệt này được xây dựng chủ yếu từ một lớp đất sét màu vàng.
Great Serpent Mound được coi là gò rắn lớn nhất thế giới. Ghi chép đầu tiên về di tích này đến từ các cuộc khảo sát được thực hiện vào thế kỷ 19 bởi Ephraim Squier và Edwin Davis. Họ đã viết về gò rắn bí ẩn này trong cuốn sách lịch sử "Di tích cổ của Thung lũng Mississippi" xuất bản năm 1848.
Trên thực tế, toàn bộ cấu trúc của gò rắn được chia thành ba phần với hình con rắn kéo dài 419 mét và rộng từ 6 đến 7,6 mét. Đầu của con rắn tiếp cận một vách đá trên một con suối, với phần thân phía sau uốn lượn qua lại.
Bản thân gò đất đặc biệt này được xây dựng chủ yếu từ một lớp đất sét màu vàng và đã được gia cố bằng một lớp đá trước khi được bao phủ bởi đất. Đầu của con rắn trông giống như đang cố ngấu nghiến một gò đất hình tròn dài khoảng 37 mét.
Đã có một số cuộc tranh luận giữa các học giả về hình dạng đặc biệt của gò đất này là một quả trứng hay Mặt trời hoặc một vật cụ thể nào đó.
Toàn bộ cấu trúc của gò rắn được chia thành ba phần với hình con rắn kéo dài.
Điều thú vị là có những gò rắn tương tự được tìm thấy ở những nơi khác trên thế giới, bao gồm cả Scotland và Canada. Và, với hình dạng thẳng đứng, với chiều cao thấp so với các chiều không gian khác của nó, gò rắn này được xếp vào cùng loại vật thể với Đường kẻ Nazca của Peru. Những cấu trúc này phù hợp để quan sát từ trên không - điều dường như là không thể trong thời đại mà nó được tạo ra.
Các nhà khảo cổ đã tranh luận về nguồn gốc của gò rắn trong nhiều thập kỷ. Nhiều cuộc khai quật đã được diễn ra, nhưng không có đồ tạo tác hoặc chôn cất nào được tìm thấy có thể trực tiếp giúp xác định thời điểm hình thành và lý do chính xác mà nó được xây dựng.
Không có đồ tạo tác hoặc chôn cất nào được tìm thấy quanh khu vực gò rắn.
Hiện tại có hai giả thuyết hàng đầu về người có thể đã xây dựng gõ rắn khổng lồ này. Một số người cho rằng nó có thể thuộc về nền văn hóa Adena, có niên đại từ năm 800 trước Công nguyên đến khoảng năm 100 sau Công nguyên.
Những người khác lại tin rằng nó được xây dựng bởi nền văn hóa Fort Ancient có từ năm 1000 đến 1750 sau Công nguyên. Giả thuyết này cũng cho rằng gò rắn khổng lồ được xây dựng vào khoảng thế kỷ 11.
Với hai giả thuyết trên, niên đại của gò rắn cũng không đồng nhất - cách nhau cả thiên niên kỷ. Vậy thì tại sao lại có sự không chắc chắn này, và tại sao lại có những giả thuyết cực kỳ khác nhau như vậy?
Văn hóa Adena là một nền văn hóa lâu đời được biết là đã phát triển mạnh mẽ ở lục địa Bắc Mỹ. William Webb, một nhà nghiên cứu nổi tiếng, đã tìm thấy bằng chứng về nền văn hóa này ở Kentucky từ đầu năm 1200 trước Công nguyên.
So sánh các đồ tạo tác được tìm thấy ở Kentucky với những đồ tạo tác được tìm thấy gần gò rắn. Nhóm nghiên cứu tin rằng nó được xây dựng bởi cùng một nền văn hóa và người ta biết rằng nền văn hóa Adena đã lan rộng đến tận Thung lũng Ohio. Đồng thời nền văn hóa Adena cũng được biết là đã xây dựng những gò đất lớn ở những nơi khác, mặc dù hình thù của chúng không giống với gò rắn.
Một nhóm tám thành viên do nhà khảo cổ học William Romain dẫn đầu đã điều tra các mẫu than từ gò rắn. Có những phát hiện xác định niên đại của việc xây dựng là từ năm 381 trước Công nguyên đến năm 44 trước Công nguyên, rất phù hợp với thời kỳ phát triển đỉnh cao của nền văn hóa Adena tại khu vực này.
Đối lập với giả thuyết này là gò rắn thuộc về nền văn hóa Fort Ancient. Năm 1996, nhóm của Robert Fletcher và Terry Cameron đã mở lại một số cuộc khai quật vào thế kỷ 19.
Họ đã tìm thấy than trong các cuộc khai quật, và khi được kiểm tra thì niên đại của những mẫu than này chỉ ở khoảng năm 1070 sau Công nguyên. Do đó, điều này dường như gợi ý rằng nền văn hóa Fort Ancient, những người sinh sống ở Thung lũng Ohio vào thời điểm đó, đã xây dựng gò rắn, và có lẽ nó đã được xây dựng đè lên trên những gò đất nhỏ hơn trước đó do nền văn hóa Adena xây dựng.
Thế nhưng bản thân giả thuyết này lại có vấn đề. Việc xây dựng gò đất không phải là đặc trưng của các dân tộc thuộc nền văn hóa Fort Ancient. Gò đất này cũng không chứa đồ tạo tác đặc trưng và cũng không có ngôi mộ đáng chú ý nào được tìm thấy gần gò rắn, điều này là bất thường đối với nền văn hóa Fort Ancient.
Tuy nhiên, có nhiều người cho rằng cả hai giả thuyết này đều có thể đúng. Có lẽ nền văn hóa Adena đã tạo ra gò rắn ban đầu, và sau đó một nghìn năm, nền văn hóa Fort Ancient đã sửa chữa những phần bị hư hại theo thời gian của gò rắn này.
Gò đất có thể đã được sử dụng để xác định thời gian hoặc sự thay đổi của các mùa.
Dựa trên nghiên cứu được tiến hành vào năm 1987, người ta cho rằng gò đất hình tròn và vùng đầu của con rắn thẳng hàng với Mặt trời lặn vào ngày hạ chí. Trong khí đó, đuôi của con rắn hướng về Mặt trời mọc vào ngày đông chí.
Điều này cho thấy rằng, nó có thể đã được sử dụng để xác định thời gian hoặc sự thay đổi của các mùa. Phương pháp này có thể đã đưa ra lời khuyên cho người dân địa phương về thời điểm gieo trồng hoặc thu hoạch mùa màng.
Ngoài ra, các đường cong trên cơ thể của con rắn đã được xác định là song song với các pha của Mặt Trăng, xen kẽ với hai điểm chí và hai điểm phân.

articles.title: NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins is the 1st Black woman to command a space mission. Will we see more diversity in the future on the final frontier?
articles.text:
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins is the 1st Black woman to command a space mission. Will we see more diversity in the future on the final frontier?
"Diversity makes the crew stronger."
When Jessica Watkins became commander of her mission to the International Space Station, she didn't just fulfill her duty as an astronaut — she made history.
Watkins is commanding SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which launched her and three other astronauts to the International Space Station on Oct. 1. As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance.
"This is certainly an important milestone, I think both for our agency and for the country," Watkins said in a press briefing ahead of Crew-13's launch.
This is Watkins' second spaceflight. She previously flew on SpaceX's Crew-4 mission in 2022 and has spent more than 200 days in space to date, though that number will keep climbing for a while, as Crew-13 is set to be an approximately six-month mission. A geologist, astronaut, aquanaut and former professional rugby player, Watkins brings an incredible variety of skills to her new role as mission commander. And, in addition to what she's bringing to her colleagues on mission, she's also providing some serious inspiration for those back on Earth.
"Jessica is an inspirational symbol to a lot of people," commercial astronaut and fellow geologist Sian Proctor, who became the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft on SpaceX's private Inspiration4 mission to orbit in September 2021, told Space.com. Sian shared that the two even crossed paths years ago, when their astronaut training aligned.
"It just means so much to so many people when you see a diverse crew, and particularly women, and women of color, in leadership positions," Proctor said. "And it means something for America."
The visibility of Watkins' accomplishments and missions carries significant cultural weight. However, in addition to recognizing her many achievements, "you also should celebrate the fact that she's African American and a role model for her community," Proctor said.
Proctor, who similarly made spaceflight history with her mission, sees Watkins' role in Crew-13 as potentially more than just an exciting moment. Hopefully, she said, it will help lay the foundation for a more diverse future in human spaceflight.
"When they announced Jessica, I was super excited because it shows progress," Proctor said, sharing that she finds incredible importance in the "idea of looking at your crew and recognizing the fact that diversity makes the crew stronger."
While Watkins' historic milestone has been celebrated on social media and across the broader media landscape, NASA did not make a public statement commemorating the historic achievement. However, the agency confirmed its pioneering nature in an email to Space.com.
"NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on her second spaceflight on Oct. 1, 2026, as commander of the agency's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station, becoming the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission," a NASA spokesperson wrote in the email.
"Watkins was selected as commander of Crew-13 based on her spaceflight experience, leadership, and ability to help the mission accomplish its objectives," the spokesperson added. "As a member of NASA's astronaut corps, she represents the best of America's talent, dedication, and spirit of exploration."
The future of spaceflight
To date, the U.S. and the Soviet Union are the only nations to have launched Black astronauts into space. (The Soviets beat the U.S. to this milestone, launching Cuba's Arnaldo Tamayo Méndez in 1980. NASA's Guion Bluford became the first Black American in space three years later.) But, as Proctor shared, perhaps moments like this could serve to inspire other nations to follow suit.
"We can be a leader in saying, Look, if your country is diverse and has people from all different backgrounds, you should be encouraging them to apply and have a chance to be selected," Proctor said.
And, as a commercial astronaut herself, Proctor added that commercial space can continue to play a vital role in diversifying spaceflight.
"Jared did not even hesitate when he offered me the mission pilot seat for Inspiration4," Proctor said of her own selection as mission pilot by Jared Isaacman, the tech billionaire who funded and commanded the SpaceX mission. He now serves as NASA administrator.
"Commercial space has opened up so much opportunity and access. We are celebrating that because that's another way in which the space industry has diversified so much," Proctor added. "You can look at the history of space exploration and who's had access, and then you look at what commercial's done in the last five years, and it's incredible."
On the topic of the future of space exploration, Proctor expressed confidence that future crewed moon landings with NASA's Artemis program will be diverse.
"NASA is going to send diverse crews to the moon because they've done a good job of selecting diverse individuals with different heritages in their background," she said. NASA's current astronaut corps is roughly 45% women and 25% people of color. However, to-date only 6 Black women (including Watkins) have ever flown to space.
"Do I want to see more? Do I want women of color? Absolutely. They only have two Black women," Proctor said. But with the current diversity in NASA's astronaut corps as well as the continued development of commercial spaceflight, she is optimistic about a diverse future on the moon.
So far, NASA's Artemis program has been making some inroads when it comes to diversity. With Artemis II, we saw four people launch to the moon which included Victor Glover, the first person of color to ever travel beyond low-Earth orbit, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen who became the first woman and first non-American to make the same leap.
Additional pressures
In reaching her own historic milestone as the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft, Proctor understands that a historic moment like this carries not just incredible significance but a fair amount of personal pressure as well.
"If something goes wrong, because of who you are, maybe your gender or your ethnicity or race, you're looked at differently," she said. "When it goes right, you're not necessarily celebrated. But if it goes wrong, then that [adds to] that whole idea of 'not being qualified,'" that can come from prejudice.
"Because of who you are and the community you represent, you become the scapegoat," she added. "So, there's pressure to not have things go wrong and do everything you can to be better than the best."
But whether or not these pressures weigh on Watkins' mind, "we're all celebrating" back on Earth, Proctor said. "We're proud of her."
Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music
