articles.title: Earliest evidence of cannabis use reveals a disturbing connection to human sacrifice victims
articles.text:
2,800-year-old tomb in Siberia has evidence of the earliest use of cannabis — possibly as a way to calm human sacrifice victims
Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.
Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.
In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.
Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.
Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.
"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.
But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.
"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.
"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."
Caspari, G., Sadykov, T., Formicheva, D., Blochin, J., Armbruster, D., Happel, O., Ryabogina, N., Boxleitner, K., Spengler, R. (2026). Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago. Science. http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta
articles.text:
Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between inflammation during pregnancy, placental damage, and autism-like traits in male mice, while females appeared naturally protected. The discovery could help explain why autism is diagnosed more frequently in boys and reveal new opportunities for early intervention.
- Share:
Scientists are still working to understand why autism develops. Genetics are known to play a major role, but researchers have also found that conditions during pregnancy can influence the likelihood of autism spectrum disorder.
A new study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory (CSHL) has uncovered a surprising connection between inflammation during pregnancy, changes in the placenta, and the development of autism-like traits in male mice. The findings suggest that certain developmental disruptions may begin much earlier than previously recognized, potentially offering new clues about autism's origins.
"To truly understand autism spectrum disorder, we have to look beyond the brain," CSHL Associate Professor Lucas Cheadle says. "Our work suggests that maternal immune activation and changes within the placenta are a gateway to autism for some unique individuals."
Scientists Identify an Early Window of Vulnerability
To investigate how inflammation affects fetal development, Cheadle and his colleagues triggered an immune response in pregnant mice at different stages of pregnancy. They used a substance that mimics the immune system's reaction to a viral infection without actually introducing a virus.
The researchers discovered that mouse fetuses were especially vulnerable when inflammation occurred 12.5 days into pregnancy. According to Irene Sanchez Martin, a postdoctoral researcher in Cheadle's laboratory, approximately one-third of the fetuses showed developmental abnormalities within just 24 hours.
Scientists have investigated the effects of maternal immune activation for decades, but these findings reveal signs of developmental disruption earlier than researchers had previously observed.
Even more striking was the difference between male and female fetuses. Across every experiment, autism-like traits appeared only in males, while females continued developing normally.
This unexpected distinction could provide insight into why autism is diagnosed substantially more often in boys than girls. What makes the finding especially intriguing is how early the difference appeared, before many of the biological changes normally associated with sex-specific development.
"It's really fascinating, because we're looking at an age which precedes hormonal surges. It precedes sexual differentiation in the brain and many other regions. So, it's surprising there would be a sex-based difference this early."
A Surprising Connection Between the Placenta and Autism
To determine why some developing mice were affected while others appeared protected, Cheadle and Sanchez Martin examined the placenta, the organ that connects a developing fetus to its mother and supports its growth throughout pregnancy.
Their attention centered on specialized cells called spongiotrophoblasts, which occupy a region of the mouse placenta where maternal and fetal cells interact.
In fetuses that developed normally, this part of the placenta remained healthy. However, male fetuses showing developmental abnormalities also had visible damage to these specialized cells.
Spongiotrophoblasts play an important role in helping the mother's immune system tolerate the developing fetus. This protection is essential because the fetus carries genetic material from both parents and is not genetically identical to the mother.
The researchers found that maternal immune activation could interfere with this protective function. When these placental cells become damaged, the mother's immune response may begin affecting the developing fetus in harmful ways.
Why Female Fetuses May Have a Hidden Advantage
The findings raise another intriguing question: Why were male fetuses vulnerable while females appeared unaffected?
One possibility is that male embryos produce distinctive proteins that can trigger an unfavorable maternal immune response following a viral infection. Another explanation is that female embryos possess some form of protection that helps them withstand inflammation during this sensitive developmental period.
Cheadle says, "A protective mechanism may exist within the female that could be harnessed to help the male. We're trying to understand how autism emerges in both sexes," he explains. "The evidence says that there are potentially different mechanisms."
These possibilities suggest that biological pathways involved in autism-like development may differ between males and females. Understanding those differences could help researchers identify why some individuals are more vulnerable to certain environmental influences during pregnancy.
Cheadle's team plans to investigate both male and female mice more closely to uncover the mechanisms responsible for these contrasting responses. Their work could eventually identify new targets for treatments and lead to strategies for intervening earlier in developmental processes associated with autism.
Although the findings come from experiments in mice and do not establish that the same mechanisms cause autism in humans, they highlight an unexpected possibility: Important clues to autism's earliest development may lie not only in the brain, but also in the placenta and its interactions with the maternal immune system.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Irene Sanchez-Martin, Bharti Kukreja, Paige Henderson, Qianyu Lin, Daniel DiMartino, Valerie Bagan, Justin Park, Brian T. Kalish, Lucas Cheadle. Maternal-fetal immune conflict contributes to male-specific impairments in a mouse model of neurodevelopmental disorders. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (38) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg0779

articles.title: Cô gái hồi sinh sau một đêm bị đóng băng khiến y học không thể lý giải
articles.text:
27 năm trước Jean Hilliard (Mỹ) bị đóng băng suốt 6 giờ đã hồi sinh kỳ diệu khiến các bác sĩ vô cùng bất ngờ.
Đêm 20/12/1980, thời tiết lạnh giá, nhiệt độ giảm xuống âm 22 độ F (-30 độ C). Jean Hilliard lúc đó 19 tuổi lái xe từ nhà bạn về nhà cha mẹ ở Lengby, Minnesota. Bất chợt, cô gái lạc tay lái và lao chệch khỏi đường. Chiếc xe dừng lại và không thể khởi động lại máy, Jean quyết định đi bộ đến nhà Wally Nelson - một người bạn, cách đó khoảng 3,2km.
Jean Hilliard lúc đó chỉ đi giày tây, khoác một chiếc áo khoác và đeo găng tay. Quần áo không đủ ấm nên Jean ngã gục xuống đường khoảng vài mét trước cửa nhà người bạn. Cô nằm bất động trong tuyết cho tới khi được Nelson phát hiện vào khoảng 7h sáng hôm sau. Thời điểm đó, người cô đã cứng như một tảng đá.
"Tôi kéo cổ áo Hilliard và đẩy vào hiên nhà. Tôi nghĩ cô ấy đã chết với cơ thể cứng hơn cả ván gỗ, nhưng tôi trông thấy vài bong bóng thoát ra từ mũi cô ấy", Wally Nelson kể lại nhiều năm sau. Nếu không nhờ phản ứng nhanh của Nelson, Hilliard có thể trở thành một trong số hàng nghìn ca tử vong do chứng hạ thân nhiệt mỗi năm. Thay vào đó, câu chuyện của cô trở thành chủ đề gây tò mò cho giới khoa học.
Theo Nytimes, các bác sĩ tại Bệnh viện Fosston sững sờ trước tình trạng của Jean. Họ cố gắng truyền dinh dưỡng cho cô qua đường tĩnh mạch nhưng cây kim không thể xuyên qua lớp da đã đóng băng. Bác sĩ cũng không thể đo nhiệt độ cho cô bằng nhiệt kế. Khuôn mặt và đôi mắt cô đông cứng, không phản ứng gì với ánh sáng. Cơ thể bệnh nhân không đáp ứng với bất kỳ hình thức chăm sóc y tế nào.
Bác sĩ George Sather điều trị cho Jean cho biết: "Cơ thể cô ấy lạnh lẽo, đông cứng giống như một miếng thịt để trong ngăn đá tủ lạnh. Các chi đều không thể gập hoặc cử động. Cô ấy không có bất kỳ một phản ứng nào trong khoảng hai hoặc ba giờ sau khi bắt đầu tan băng. Nhịp tim của Jean chỉ đập 8 lần mỗi phút. Nhiệt độ cơ thể khoảng 26 độ C".
Bác sĩ bó tay trước trường hợp của Jean.
Các bác sĩ lắc đầu bất lực. Họ nói các tế bào hoàn toàn đông cứng, các cơ quan nội tạng cũng lạnh dần, sẽ càng khó hơn để chúng có thể thực hiện chức năng của mình cho tới khi hoàn toàn ngừng hẳn. Thậm chí não cũng không thể cứu. Jean sẽ không còn hy vọng nào cả. Điều duy nhất các bác sĩ có thể làm cho cô gái trẻ là đắp các túi giữ ấm quanh người cô để nâng nhiệt độ cơ thể lên, làm tan lớp băng.
11h trưa, Jean bắt đầu co giật và lấy lại được ý thức một cách thần kỳ. Mọi người xung quanh cô đều kinh ngạc. Vào ban đêm, cô có thể di chuyển đôi cánh tay. Đến ngày thứ 3, đôi chân của cô cũng có thể di chuyển. Cô phải điều trị y tế trong 49 ngày tiếp theo nhưng sau đó hồi phục hoàn toàn và không phải cắt bỏ ngay cả một ngón tay.
Đến nay, không ai biết được làm cách nào mà cơ thể của cô gái lại có thể phục hồi hoàn toàn khỏi trạng thái đóng băng cứng như vậy. Trường hợp của Jean Hilliard hiện vẫn còn là một bí ẩn của ngành y.
Vì sao một cơ thể có thể sống sót trong trạng thái rắn khi bị đông lạnh?
Không giống như nhiều vật chất, nước chiếm một thể tích lớn khi ở thể rắn, và thậm chí còn nhiều hơn cả khi ở thể lỏng.
Sự giãn nở theo nhiệt độ này là một tin xấu đối với các mô tế bào bị nhiễm lạnh, vì chất lỏng bên trong cơ thể có nguy cơ bị phồng lên đến mức làm vỡ tung các mạch máu, hay xuyên thủng màng tế bào.
Nhiều loài động vật tiến hóa một số cách thích nghi để đối phó mối đe dọa từ tinh thể băng sắc nhọn trong điều kiện dưới 0 độ C. Loài cá biển sâu có tên cá băng vây đen Nam Cực sản sinh glycoprotein như một loại chất chống đông tự nhiên. Ếch gỗ biến thành phần trong tế bào thành sirô bằng cách để glucose tràn ngập cơ thể, nhờ đó có khả năng chống đóng băng và mất nước. Ở bên ngoài tế bào, nước chuyển tự do thành thể rắn, bao bọc mô trong băng và khiến ếch gỗ trông như những khối băng hình con ếch.
Tuy nhiên, cơ thể của Hilliard lại chưa gặp phải những tình trạng này. Theo lý giải của khoa học, rất có thể nạn nhân dù bị hạ thân nhiệt, nhưng vẫn có nhiệt độ cao hơn nhiều so với mức đóng băng.
Jean Hilliard (ở giữa) quay trở lại cuộc sống bình thường sau tai nạn. (Ảnh: MPR News).
Nếu cơ thể người bị lạnh sẽ xuất hiện hiện tượng hạ thân nhiệt. Sự nguy hiểm của hiện tượng hạ thân nhiệt phụ thuộc vào từng mức độ giảm nhiệt cơ thể. Cụ thể khi xuống mức 32 độ C, cơ chế bù trừ nhiệt độ của cơ thể bắt đầu suy giảm, trạng thái tâm thần có thể biến đổi và thậm chí người bệnh có thể bị mất trí nhớ. Khi xuống mức 27 độ C, nạn nhân bắt đầu mất ý thức. Khi còn dưới 21 độ C, trạng thái hạ thân nhiệt nặng sẽ diễn ra, và có thể dẫn tới tử vong.
Kỷ lục ghi nhận thân nhiệt thấp nhất của một người trưởng thành mà vẫn sống sót là ở 13,7 độ C. Ở thời điểm đó, người này đã bị ngâm trong nước lạnh và đóng băng trong thời gian khá lâu.
Trên thực tế, cơ thể người hay bất kỳ loài động vật nào cũng sẽ trở nên căng cứng một cách rõ rệt khi gặp phải tình trạng hạ thân nhiệt nghiêm trọng. Điều này dễ gây nhầm lẫn với tình trạng đóng băng, dù mức độ nghiêm trọng của 2 trạng thái này là khác nhau.
Đối với Hilliard, cơ thể của cô có lẽ đã gặp phải tình trạng căng cứng giống như khi xảy ra với một xác chết. Điểm lợi của trạng thái này đó là cơ thể sẽ tự động "đóng" các kênh dẫn đến mạch máu dưới da, nhằm giữ cho các cơ quan bên trong vẫn hoạt động ổn định.
Cơ chế này hoạt động hiệu quả đến mức rất dễ khiến người ta lầm tưởng rằng nạn nhân đã chết, với biểu hiện hoàn toàn lạnh ngắt khi chạm vào và không có dấu hiệu của sự sống. Thậm chí nhịp tim cũng được đưa về ở mức rất thấp.
Khi cơ thể rơi vào trạng thái này, các nhân viên y tế sẽ rất khó để cứu giúp nạn nhân, vì họ không thể dùng kim tiêm để xuyên qua lớp da do các tĩnh mạch bị co thắt nặng nề, và tình trạng mất nước khiến chúng ép chặt vào các cơ bên trong.
Nạn nhân lúc này cũng ở trạng thái cực kỳ nguy hiểm, và cận kề cái chết nếu như không có sự can thiệp kịp thời.
Những điều này cho thấy Hilliard đã hoàn toàn may mắn và sống sót một cách thần kỳ khi cô thực sự đã "đối mặt với tử thần".
Câu chuyện cũng cho thấy những điều tuyệt vời mà cơ thể con người có thể đạt được. Dẫu vậy, chúng ta không nên trông chờ vào may mắn, vì rất ít người có khả năng chịu đựng sự thay đổi trạng thái khắc nghiệt tới như vậy.

articles.title: 400-year-old padlock discovered in shipwreck off Wales finally opened
articles.text:
Cryptic padlock from a 400-year-old shipwreck finally opened — but it leaves a mystery
Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.
An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.
The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.
Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.
Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.
To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.
"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"
Smugglers' ship
The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.
A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.
Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.
Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.
"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."
- Wreck of World War II Japanese 'hellship' that sank with more than 1,000 Allied POWs on board discovered off the Philippines
- First shipwrecks linked to real pirates of the Caribbean found in Bahamas
- Divers find marble treasure from Athens' Acropolis in Lord Elgin's shipwrecked brig at the bottom of the Aegean Sea
Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.
The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.
"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."
Patrick Pester is the trending news writer at Live Science. His work has appeared on other science websites, such as BBC Science Focus and Scientific American. Patrick retrained as a journalist after spending his early career working in zoos and wildlife conservation. He was awarded the Master's Excellence Scholarship to study at Cardiff University where he completed a master's degree in international journalism. He also has a second master's degree in biodiversity, evolution and conservation in action from Middlesex University London. When he isn't writing news, Patrick investigates the sale of human remains.

articles.title: NASA announces experimental X-70 Fractal aircraft: A 'new beginning for aeronautics'
articles.text:
NASA announces experimental X-70 Fractal aircraft: A 'new beginning for aeronautics'
"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly."
NASA has revealed a glimpse of its next X-plane, known as the X-70 Fractal.
Or at least what it thinks the X-70 will look like once built. The agency released a short statement on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announcing the X-plane, or experimental plane, declaring it to be a highly maneuverable test bed with a "rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology," allowing NASA to swap both external and internal components on-the-fly. This modular architecture will allow NASA to "explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight," according to the agency's statement.
The announcement was made alongside an AI-generated image showing two canted vertical tail fins emerging from swirling smoke. Little can be gleaned from the image about what final form the X-70 might take, but the tail fins are somewhat reminiscent of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor or Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.
"The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the statement. The NASA chief called the aircraft "just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics" and said that the agency expects the X-70 to make its first flight within two years.
"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly," Isaacman added.
NASA's statement fleshes out a few details about the X-70's capabilities. According to the agency, Fractal will fly at a cruise speed of Mach .75, about the same as a Boeing 737 Classic. The X-70 will be able to reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet (13.7 kilometers), and will have a range exceeding 1,726 miles (2,777 kilometers, or 1,500 nautical miles).
The X-70 Fractal will also be able to carry around 2,000 pounds (900 kg) of experimental payloads both internally and externally, which will allow for a "wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities," NASA said in the statement.
NASA adds it will have a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds (4,535 kilograms), around the same weight as the Scaled Composites- and Northrop Grumman-developed Model 437 Vanguard experimental aircraft. In fact, the two aircraft share a similar silhouette — at least in the AI image of the X-70 Fractal NASA has released so far.
The agency's most recent X-plane, the X-59, has been flying for over a year. That jet features a radical long-nosed geometry without a forward windscreen; pilots fly by way of an augmented reality screen that combines views from sensors and a forward-facing camera.
That geometry dampens the shockwaves coming off of the X-59 when it flies faster than the sound barrier, allowing it to fly at speeds over Mach 1 without the thunderous sonic booms that typically accompany supersonic flight.
There are numerous experimental aircraft being developed by private companies, such as Boom Supersonic's X-1 jet, which, like the X-59, aims to develop technologies that lessen the auditory impact of sonic booms on the ground.
In terms of other government X-plane projects, Boeing is working on the F-47, a next-generation stealth fighter for use by the U.S. military, and DARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, has an X-plane project of its own known as CRANE.
Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

articles.title: Tuổi thọ của loài người có thể đạt tới 1.000, chuyên gia: Chìa khóa ở tế bào bất tử này!
articles.text:
Theo "Thần tiên truyện" thì Bành Tổ là cháu 6 đời của vua Chuyên Húc. Ông là người sống tới 767 tuổi mà vẫn còn khỏe mạnh. Ông đã trải qua nhà Hạ đến tận cuối thời nhà Ân và còn được mời giữ chức Đại phu. Thế nhưng tới sau thời nhà Thương và nhà Chu, trong sử sách hay truyền thuyết không còn thấy ghi lại ai sống trường thọ như vậy nữa.
Tuy nhiên, sau đó các nhà khảo cổ đã phát hiện ra rằng, vào thời cổ đại, người xưa sử dụng cách tính 1 năm là 60 ngày, tức là 60 ngày sẽ được coi là 1 năm tuổi. Vì thế, tuổi thật của Bành Tổ chỉ đạt khoảng 127 tuổi. Dù vậy thì đối với hậu thế, một người có thể sống khỏe mạnh tới hơn 100 tuổi như Bành Tổ đã được coi là kỳ tích.
Từ câu chuyện này, nhiều nhà khoa học bắt đầu theo đuổi việc nghiên cứu về các mã gen trường thọ của con người. Trong thế giới hiện đại, nhờ các công nghệ mới như trí tuệ nhân tạo, công nghệ y học phát triển thì tuổi thọ của loài người ngày càng cao. Vậy theo cách tính của họ thì tuổi thọ giới hạn của con người là bao lâu?
Ngay từ thế kỉ XIX, nhà thống kê học người Anh Benjamin Gompertz đã tính ra định luật tử vong của 1 người và gọi nó là định luật Gompertz-Makeham. Theo định luật này, tỷ lệ tử vong của 1 người sẽ tăng lên gấp đôi sau mỗi 8 năm kể từ khi người đó bước qua độ tuổi 30.
Để chống lại sự lão hóa, con người bắt đầu theo đuổi việc tìm kiếm sự trường sinh bất lão. (Ảnh: Baidu)
Văn phòng Thống kê của vương quốc Anh đã đưa ra dự đoán rằng con người trong tương lai sẽ đạt mức tuổi thọ trung bình là 100. Theo dự báo này, phụ nữ ở Anh quốc sẽ đạt tuổi thọ bình quân 100 tuổi vào năm 2055, và nam giới đạt tuổi thọ 100 vào năm 2080.
Theo nghiên cứu được đăng tải trên tạp chí Royal Society Open Science, nhóm nghiên cứu của Viện Công nghệ Liên bang Thụy Sĩ ở Lausanne (EPFL) đã sử dụng phương pháp ngoại suy để phân tích các dữ liệu hiện có. Họ đã thu thập được dữ liệu về tuổi thọ của hơn 1.100 người "siêu thọ" tại 13 quốc gia. Ngoài ra họ còn thu thập dữ liệu của những người cao tuổi tại Ý trong các năm từ 2009 đến 2015. Kết quả của cuộc nghiên cứu cho thấy, con người có thể sống ít nhất tới 130 tuổi hoặc lâu hơn nữa. Tuy tỷ lệ này thấp nhưng không phải là không có.
Kết quả này cũng khá tương đồng với nghiên cứu của các giáo sư từ đại học Matxcova cùng Viện Sinh học biển Nga đã thực hiện dựa trên các sinh vật biển. Trong nghiên cứu của họ, cá mập Greenland là loài có tuổi thọ trung bình nhiều nhất. Tuổi thọ trung bình của chúng là 392 năm, cao nhất lên tới 512 năm. Họ cũng tính toán ra tuổi thọ cao nhất của loài người là khoảng 168 tuổi.
Kể từ khi công nghệ sinh học phát triển, các nhà khoa học đã luôn nghiên cứu về các tế bào, họ nhận thấy rằng sự già đi của con người có liên quan tới sự phân chia tế bào. Khi các tế bào già và chết đi thì cũng là lúc con người đi tới hồi kết. Cụ thể, đó là đoạn DNA có trình tự lặp lại nhiều lần ở đầu mỗi nhiễm sắc thể tên là Telomere. Chúng đóng vai trò chủ chốt trong quá trình lão hóa sinh học. Trong phần lớn tế bào, độ dài của telomere giảm dần theo tuổi cơ thể.
Mỗi khi một tế bào phân chia, chiều dài của telomere sẽ giảm một chút. Cuối cùng, khi telomere ngắn tới một mức nào đó, tế bào sẽ chết. Elizabeth Blackburn, nhà sinh học tế bào người Mỹ gốc Australia từng đoạt giải Nobel Y học đã ví các telomere giống như đầu mút của dây giày. Khi đầu mút hỏng hoặc văng ra, dây giày bắt đầu sờn và hỏng.
Tiến sĩ Ronald DePinho và nhóm cộng sự đã thành công trong thí nghiệm "cải lão hoàn đồng" trên chuột. (Ảnh: Đại học Harvard)
Không cam tâm với kết quả này, một nhóm các nhà khoa học Mỹ thuộc Viện ung thư Dana-Farber ở Ɓoston đã bắt tay vào tìm kiếm bí mật của sự trường sinh bất lão. Sau đó, tiến sĩ Ronald DePinho và các cộng sự củɑ ông đã tìm thấy sự đột phá về việc chống lão hóa giúp con người duy trì thanh xuân mãi mãi. Nội dung củɑ nghiên cứu này đã được đăng tải trên tạp chí Ɲature.
Nhóm của tiến sĩ Ronald DePinho đã đảo ngược được các tác động củɑ sự lão hoá đối với động vật thông quɑ những thử nghiệm trên loài chuột. Họ đã tạo ra những con chuột mɑng gen chứa enzym telomerase có thể kiểm soát được. Loại enzym có tên telomerase này chính là enzym giúp cho telomere duy trì. Những con chuột mang enzym này đều lão hóa rất sớm.
Từ những con chuột này, các nhà nghiên cứu đã xác định được rằng, nếu tái kích hoạt lượng enzym telomerase thì các đoạn telomere sẽ được khôi phục và các triệu chứng của tuổi già cũng sẽ giảm đi. Chỉ trong 2 tháng được cho sử dụng thuốc tăng lượng enzym telomerase, những con chuột này đã phát triển nhiều tế bào mới đến mức có thể coi như "cải lão hoàn đồng".
Sau khi nhóm của tiến sĩ Ronald DePinho công bố kết quả cuộc nghiên cứu này, giới khoa học đã nổ ra nhiều tranh cãi. Tuy nhiên, xét trên thực tế, thí nghiệm vẫn chỉ là mới thực hiện trên động vật và chỉ mang tính lý thuyết.
Vào năm 2015, Tiến sĩ Aubrey de Grey - nhà lão khoa người Anh, người sáng lập dự án giảm thiểu quá trình lão hóa (SENS) có trụ sở tại Mỹ đã làm rúng động thế giới khi tuyên bố rằng con người có thể sống thọ tới 1.000 tuổi tại 1 hội thảo khoa học.
Sở dĩ tuyên bố này gây ra làn sóng dư luận là bởi con số này dường như nằm ngoài tầm với của loài người. Thế nhưng Tiến sĩ Aubrey de Grey đã đưa ra dẫn chứng về tế bào bất tử Hela. Theo ông, tiền đề của quá trình lão hóa của con người là do tế bào chết đi sau khoảng 56 lần phân chia. Tuy nhiên, tế bào Hela khác với tế bào bình thường của con người bởi nó chính là tế bào bất tử.
Tế bào này tình cờ được tạo ra bởi George Otto Gey, một nhà khoa học tại bệnh viện Johns Hopkins, Maryland, Mỹ vào năm 1951. Ông lấy mẫu từ một người phụ nữ da đen mắc bệnh ung thư tên là Henrietta Lacks. Sau đó, các nhà khoa học đã đặt tên cho tế bào là Hela và nó nhanh chóng trở thành mẫu vật vô giá với y khoa toàn cầu.
Theo tiến sĩ Aubrey de Grey, tế bào Hela là chìa khóa của sự bất tử của con người. (Ảnh: Baidu)
Khác với các tế bào người bình thường, tế bào Hela có thể tồn tại và sinh sản bình thường trong phòng thí nghiệm. Các nhà khoa học đã sử dụng chúng trong nghiên cứu vắc xin bại liệt, thử nghiệm trong môi trường không trọng lực, nhân bản, tạo bản đồ gen và nuôi cấy mô.
Với giới y học, việc sở hữu tế bào bất tử là vô cùng quan trọng trong nghiên cứu. Cho đến nay, ngoài tế bào Hela, chưa ai tìm ra tế bào bất tử nào khác. Kể từ sau khi bước sang thế kỷ 21 tới nay, đã có 5 công trình nghiên cứu dựa trên tế bào Hela đoạt giải Nobel. Và tiến sĩ Aubrey de Grey cho rằng nếu khám phá được bí mật của tế bào Hela, con người có thể sống tới 1.000 tuổi.
Nhưng các nhà khoa học cũng đưa ra băn khoăn rằng liệu loài người khi duy trì được sự bất tử có thực sự tốt hay không? Họ cho rằng không có sự sống bất tử trên Trái đấy là có lý do riêng của nó. Nếu loài người có thể bất tử, dân số sẽ tăng lên quá nhiều, tài nguyên cạn kiệt và tất cả chúng ta cũng như Trái đất đều sẽ bị hủy hoại nghiêm trọng.

articles.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
articles.text:
Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- Texas A&M University
- Summary:
- A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.
- Share:
For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.
However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.
Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.
Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success
To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.
The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.
Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.
"One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension."
Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading
Auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.
Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.
Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.
The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.
What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read
The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.
For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.
"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky said. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together."
The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.
According to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Ryan McCullar. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Daniel B. Hajovsky, Christopher R. Niileksela, Dawn P. Flanagan, Vincent C. Alfonso, William Joel Schneider, Jacob Robbins. Toward a Consensus Model of Cognitive–Reading Achievement Relations Using Meta-Structural Equation Modeling. Journal of Intelligence, 2025; 13 (8): 104 DOI: 10.3390/jintelligence13080104

articles.title: 'Very rare' strain of leprosy found in man's 1,600-year-old burial in Germany
articles.text:
1,600-year-old burial holds remains of man infected with a 'very rare' strain of leprosy in Germany
A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.
Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.
This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.
"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."
In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.
The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.
"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."
A rare form of leprosy
To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."
The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.
But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.
"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."
While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.
Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: China lays out plans to land astronauts on the moon 'before 2030.' Can NASA still win this race?
articles.text:
China lays out plans to land astronauts on the moon 'before 2030.' Can NASA still win this race?
China has given us some details about the epic moon landing it plans to pull off a few years from now.
Chinese officials laid out the roadmap for its crewed lunar campaign at the 7th Manned Space Symposium, which was held Oct. 31 and Nov. 1 in Beijing. The campaign consists of four missions, culminating in a crewed touchdown "before 2030," according to media reports.
That timeline — which is consistent with previous statements made by the China Manned Space Agency — keeps the pressure on the U.S., which aims to put its own astronauts down on the moon in 2028, via NASA's Artemis program.
China shooting for the moon
The first mission in China's four-part lunar campaign is scheduled to fly in 2027, according to CNSpaceflight, an X account that keeps a close eye on China's activities in space. The outlet cited an X user who shared a presentation slide of the plan.
That launch — the first of of China's new Long March 10A rocket — will send an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO) for a series of tests. Mengzhou, whose name means "Dream Vessel," is the next-gen crew capsule that will carry Chinese astronauts to lunar orbit.
Mission number two, launching in 2028, will involve a different set of hardware — the more powerful Long March 10 rocket and the Lanyue ("Embracing the Moon") lunar lander. This will also be an uncrewed flight, and it will mark the debut of the Long March 10, which will send Lanyue to orbit around the moon. If all goes to plan, Lanyue will touch down on the moon and then launch itself back to lunar orbit.
Mission number three, flying in 2029, will also target an uncrewed lunar landing, but it will feature two Long March 10 launches — one apiece for Mengzhou and Lanyue. The two spacecraft will conduct a rendezvous and docking rehearsal in lunar orbit, then separate for Lanyue's trip down to the surface.
This will set the stage for mission four — the real deal, in which two Long March 10s launch a crewed Mengzhou and an uncrewed Lanyue "before 2030." The two vessels will dock in lunar orbit, and the astronauts will move into Lanyue for their historic lunar landing.
Three astronauts will apparently launch on Mengzhou, and two of them will land on the moon aboard Lanyue, according to CNSpaceflight. The duo will spend three days on the lunar surface, conducting moonwalks on each of those days.
And about that "before 2030" timeline: The wording may have been chosen very carefully.
"One reading is that 2029 coincides with the 80th anniversary of the current government, creating a strong internal incentive to achieve the landing that year. At the same time, the technical schedule (new Long March 10 family, Mengzhou, Lanyue, dual-launch operations) remains aggressive; committing publicly to 2029 would create significant political exposure if any major test slips," CNSpaceflight wrote in a Nov. 2 X post.
"Using 'before 2030' therefore functions as deliberate wording flexibility: a 2029 landing can still be presented as an early historic success, while a slip into 2030 remains inside the stated goal without requiring a formal target revision. You just need to put 'year-end' after 'before 2030,'" the outlet added.
NASA's plan
NASA's Artemis program has already sent astronauts around the moon, doing so this past April on the Artemis II mission. The agency is currently gearing up for Artemis III, a crewed flight to LEO that will test rendezvous and docking procedures between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the Artemis program's two private crewed landers — SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.
Artemis III is currently on track to fly in the summer of 2027, NASA officials have said. But an on-time liftoff is far from guaranteed, as both Starship and Blue Moon still have some boxes to check.
Starship just reached Earth orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, for example, and it has yet to demonstrate off-Earth refueling, which will be a crucial part of any Starship mission beyond Earth orbit. And Blue Moon has yet to leave the ground at all. The Blue Origin lander is scheduled to fly for the first time next spring, on an uncrewed test mission that will send it to the lunar surface.
If all goes well on Artemis III, NASA will be clear to start prepping for Artemis IV, which will put astronauts down near the lunar south pole aboard either Starship or Blue Moon. (It's unclear at the moment which lander NASA will choose.)
NASA is currently targeting early 2028 for the launch of Artemis IV. If that schedule holds, the agency will beat China and pull off the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 back in 1972.
But the new moon race won't end there, because this one isn't all about flags and footprints. Both NASA and China aim to build bases on the lunar surface over the next decade or so, setting up humanity's first true outpost on a world beyond Earth. The stakes are high, NASA and U.S. military officials have stressed: Whoever does so first can claim the best spots and get the best access to key lunar resources such as water ice. The leader will also get to establish norms of behavior on the moon, which at the moment is a bit of a Wild West of exploration.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: Bạn sang nhà chơi phát hiện "núi vàng, núi bạc hơn 100 tỷ": Chưa kịp vui mừng tình bạn lâu năm đã sứt mẻ!
articles.text:
Một kho báu toàn vàng và bạc cổ từng được phát hiện trên mảnh đất của một người nông dân khiến thế giới ngỡ ngàng.
Khu vực phát hiện kho báu.
Vào năm 2009, một kho báu toàn vàng và bạc cổ đã được phát hiện trên một mảnh đất nông nghiệp tại Anh và trở nên nổi tiếng. Cụ thể, khi đi qua mảnh đất của nông dân Fred Johnson, người đàn ông tên Terry Herbert đã phát hiện ra kho báu Anglo-Saxon trị giá 3,3 triệu Bảng Anh (hơn 102 tỷ đồng theo tỷ giá hiện tại) nhờ máy dò kim loại.
Terry Herbert đã phát hiện ra kho báu Anglo-Saxon trị giá 3,3 triệu Bảng Anh nhờ máy dò kim loại.
Kho báu này được đặt tên là Staffordshire Hoard và được cho là có tới 3.900 cổ vật - một trong những kho báu Anglo-Saxon lớn nhất từ trước đến nay ở Anh.
Kho báu này có tới 3900 cổ vật.
Nhà khảo cổ học thuộc Hội đồng Hạt Staffordshire cho biết kho báu quý khổng lồ có ít nhất 650 món đồ bằng vàng, nặng hơn 5kg vàng nguyên chất và 530 món đồ bằng bạc nặng hơn 1kg. Hầu hết được cho là thuộc về hoàng gia hoặc quý tộc.
Một trong những hiện vật của kho báu khổng lồ.
Kho báu này đã được bán cho các viện bảo tàng, đem lại sự giàu có cho Fred Johnson và Terry Herbert. Nhưng theo Daily Mail, sau hơn 1 thập kỷ họ vẫn đang tranh chấp về các khoản phân chia tiền mặt. Ông Herbert nói rằng ông Johnson muốn tất cả cho riêng mình.
Ông Herbert thậm chí còn cho biết việc tìm thấy kho báu chính là một lời nguyền và nó đã hủy hoại tình bạn của hai người.
Theo Daily Mail, Bảo tàng Birmingham và Phòng trưng bày nghệ thuật bảo tàng Potteries đã cùng mua kho báu giá trị này.

articles.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
articles.text:
All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
- Date:
- November 3, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.
- Share:
A new study reveals all five fundamental nucleobases – the molecular “letters” of life – have been detected in samples from the asteroid Ryugu.
Asteroid particles offer a glimpse into the chemical ingredients that may have helped kindle life on Earth. The Ryugu samples were returned from space in 2020 by Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s (JAXA) Hayabusa2 mission.
In 2023, an international team reported they had found one of the nucleobases in these samples – uracil. Now, in a study published in Nature Astronomy, a team of Japanese scientists has confirmed all five nucleobases are present in this pristine asteroid material.
This means these ingredients for life may have been widespread throughout the Solar System in its early years.
Why look for nucleobases?
Nucleobases are nitrogen-containing organic molecules that form the “letters” of genetic information in DNA and RNA. The five main nucleobases are adenine and guanine (known as purines), as well as cytosine, thymine and uracil (known as pyrimidines).
These molecules combine with sugars and phosphates to yield nucleotides – the building blocks of genetic material. Without nucleobases, the genetic code that allows organisms to grow, reproduce and evolve would not exist.
By studying purines and pyrimidines in Ryugu samples, scientists can reconstruct the chemical history of primitive asteroids. In turn, this gives us a better understanding of how the building blocks of life may have been formed and existed across the Solar System.
Hayabusa2 delivered a total of 5.4 grams of pristine asteroid material. Researchers have to use ultra-clean lab conditions to avoid contaminating it. They extracted organic molecules using water and hydrocholoric acid, and then purified them for further detection.
They found all five nucleobases in the two Ryugu samples they analysed, in roughly similar amounts.
Key components of genetic material – in space
The new results align with previous findings on space rocks. The Murchison meteorite that fell in Australia in 1969, and the Orgueil meteorite in France, 1864, have previously yielded a rich variety of organic molecules, including nucleobases.
Of course, meteorites that land on Earth can be contaminated by their journey and landing. But pristine samples from NASA’s mission to asteroid Bennu also yielded all five nucleobases in 2025.
Asteroids such as Ryugu, Bennu, and the parent body of the Orgueil meteorite are remnants of the early Solar System. They can preserve materials largely unchanged for about 4.5 billion years.
Interestingly, these asteroids show chemical differences. Murchison is enriched in purines, while Bennu and Orgueil contain more pyrimidines. It is thought this balance may be influenced by ammonia, a key molecule that can shape which nucleobases can form.
By peering into Ryugu’s relatively pristine samples and comparing them with meteorites like Murchison and Orgueil, researchers are tracing the cosmic journey of life’s probable molecular ingredients.
Their results suggest key components of genetic material may have formed in space and later delivered to the early Earth. In other words, the story of life on our planet may be deeply connected to the chemistry of such ancient asteroids.
A path for the ingredients of life
Together, these discoveries show that carbon-rich asteroids throughout the Solar System contain diverse prebiotic chemistry. However, the precise mixture of molecules – such as the balance between purines and pyrimidines – varies depending on the asteroid’s chemical environment and history.
Because the Ryugu samples were collected directly in space and protected from Earth’s contamination, they provide one of the clearest views of ancient Solar System chemistry.
The discovery of all five nucleobases on Ryugu suggests the molecular ingredients of life may have been already forming in space billions of years ago. Asteroids may have helped deliver those ingredients to the early Earth – making the origin of life part of a much larger cosmic chemical story.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Kliti Grice, John Curtin Distinguished Professor of Organic and Isotope Geochemistry, Curtin University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Toshiki Koga, Yasuhiro Oba, Yoshinori Takano, Hiroshi Naraoka, Nanako O. Ogawa, Kazunori Sasaki, Hajime Sato, Toshihiro Yoshimura, Naohiko Ohkouchi. A complete set of canonical nucleobases in the carbonaceous asteroid (162173) Ryugu. Nature Astronomy, 2026; 10 (5): 655 DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02791-z

articles.title: From forest trails to 'Sims for Bears,' researchers are learning how grizzlies navigate a fragmented wilderness
articles.text:
'We’re looking at how a bear sees the world': From forest trails to 'Sims for Bears,' researchers are learning how grizzlies navigate a fragmented wilderness
Scientists in the U.S. and Canada are decoding grizzly bears' behavior to learn how they navigate a human-dominated world. What they find could build a safer future for both species.
Across 53 challenging days between fall 2020 and spring 2021, a 360-pound (160 kilograms) young male grizzly bear nicknamed "Lingenpolter" tried to cross Interstate 90 in western Montana 46 times. High-resolution GPS tracking showed him moving parallel to four lanes of roaring traffic, bouncing off the highway like a furry pinball as he searched for a gap.
Eventually, Lingenpolter beat the odds, probably by slipping under a river bridge. But his hero's journey shows what a formidable barrier a busy highway can be for wildlife, Cecily Costello, a research wildlife biologist at Montana's Department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks, told Live Science. "It is easy to imagine the difficulty this grizzly bear experienced trying to reach the other side," Costello said.
This past May, another grizzly wasn't so lucky. Braving a crossing near one of Lingenpolter's attempts, the 27-year-old male bear was struck and killed by a truck, triggering a multicar rollover.
It's crucial for grizzly bears (Ursus arctos), also known as brown bears, to have room to roam. When they can't move between populations to mate, small groups get genetically isolated. And what's true for bears can also be true for other wildlife. "It's really challenging to be a small, fragmented population," said Michael Proctor, a wildlife biologist at Birchdale Ecological Ltd., a Canada-based environmental consulting firm. Such fragmentation is "one of the mechanisms by which we lose entire communities, and sometimes whole species," he told Live Science.
Nowhere is this challenge more urgent than in the 2,100 mile long (3,400 kilometers) region stretching along the spine of the Rocky Mountains between Yellowstone in Wyoming and the Yukon in northern Canada. The area, which spans five U.S. states, two Canadian provinces, and more than 75 Indigenous territories "represents the most intact, connected, wild, large mountain region in the world," Jordan Reeves, program director of landscape connectivity at the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative (Y2Y), which aims to secure connectivity throughout the region told Live Science.
But as highways, rail lines, and human development fragment its valleys, maintaining connected pathways for grizzly bears across this landscape has become a challenge.
Grizzlies range across vast, diverse terrain, spanning high-elevation alpine habitats, mid-mountain slopes, and low valley bottoms, which means safeguarding their movement can also protect passageways for coexisting species, including wolverines, mountain goats, elk and bighorn sheep, Proctor said. That's why researchers are trying to understand why, where and when grizzlies move. And what stops them in their tracks.
"We're looking at how a bear sees the world," Andrew Derocher, a bear biologist at the University of Alberta who has used GPS collars on grizzly bears to trace their movements, told Live Science.
Nature versus nurture
When Sarah Sells started her graduate studies in animal behavior, her supervisor told her to "try to crawl into their fur brains and understand how they think," Sells told Live Science. Although we can't recreate exactly what's going on between a grizzly's ears, GPS collars that track animal movement hourly can tell scientists a lot about how animals behave, said Sells, who is currently the assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey's Montana Cooperative Wildlife Research Unit.
That tracking data is starting to produce an incredibly detailed picture not just of where bears go but also how and why they're making those choices.
"Bears are food finding machines," Chris Servheen, a bear biologist with the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Bear Specialist Group, told Live Science. "So remembering where they found food is critical to their success in life."
Using a combination of telemetry data (information collected by tracking devices) and movement modeling, Derocher and colleagues have investigated how well grizzlies remember where food is and when it is best to visit a foraging patch. Derocher's research showed that about two-thirds of the bears have a great memory for where and in what season they previously found food. His tracking data also revealed that wild bears generally avoid humans. But bears have only a few months to fatten up for winter. If food is scarce, many bears go into human environments and sometimes get killed, Proctor said.
The data is also offering insight into different bear "personalities." Bears are ultimately individuals, with their own traits and quirks, Servheen said.
Tracking data suggests that a lot of bear behavior is transmitted culturally via a mother's influence. Sometimes, the wrong behavior can get passed down to the next generation, Servheen said. For example, an infamous female grizzly known as 399 jaywalked potentially hundreds of times in the Jackson Hole valley in Wyoming while managing to keep her distance from humans. Her 20-odd cubs learned to follow her example, but they lacked her strategic caution. Several were killed by vehicles or management euthanizations.
"It's a risky thing to teach your kids to do stuff like that," Servheen said. "And her offspring weren't as smart as she was."
A cracked windshield
Further north along the region between Yellowstone and the Yukon, Proctor's first DNA survey across 1,500 square miles (4,000 square kilometers) of southern British Columbia in the late 1990s shattered his illusion that the bears, along with bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis) and other species in this province, were free to roam. Instead, he found a "cracked windshield" landscape, where roads and human sprawl had fractured the wilderness into isolated genetic islands. In the 2000s, the genetic diversity of the South Selkirk grizzly bears — a detatched subpopulation inhabiting southeastern British Columbia, northern Idaho, and northeastern Washington — was so low, for example, that biologists feared the bears wouldn't survive.
But Proctor and his colleagues went on to use bear movement data to model pathways through human-settled valleys. Proctor was so convinced about the viability of one potential corridor that he paid 10,000 Canadian dollars ($7,000) of his own money to buy a key piece of land right in the middle of it. "That was the first canoe over the waterfall of purchasing connectivity land," Proctor said
Proctor’s land secured a segment of a crucial connectivity corridor and, in the following years, he and other scientists partnered with trusts to purchase other land parcels, build fences, and establish safe corridors for grizzlies in the Creston Valley in southeastern British Columbia. These actions helped bears move north and south (sometimes across the border) and between the South Selkirk Mountains and Purcell Mountains. The researchers then watched bears like "Captain Hook," who'd been shot in the leg, hobble into the South Selkirks and breed with eight females. By 2021, nine immigrant bears had produced 27 new offspring within the population.
"This is gene flow; this is connectivity," Proctor said. "We took a completely isolated population and pretty much recovered it."
Despite efforts to safeguard corridors through human occupied landscape, roads continue to stop bears in their tracks. When Servheen tracked bears near Highway 2 in northwest Montana, he found that many of the grizzlies avoided the highway altogether and those that crossed did so at night. But he also found that the bears' crossings clustered in specific sections of the road. Finding the crossing zones has helped researchers identify good locations for constructing overpasses and underpasses on many busy highways, but a crossing structure on its own is not enough, Servheen cautioned.
A bear's memory for where to find food is exemplary, but there's no special reward in a bear's brain for crossing a road safely — only a fatal penalty when they don't, Servheen said. So conservationists can't rely on bears to remember where crossings are. Instead, they must build fencing along the highway to funnel wildlife into the underpasses or overpasses. Then, the immediate land on each side needs to allow animals safe passage. "Otherwise, you have a bridge to nowhere," Servheen said.
Now researchers such as Sells are trying to use data about bears' likeliest routes to determine potential corridors in locations where they have little tracking data or where few bears live yet.
To do this, Sells is developing a virtual "Sims for Bears" that recreates the Continental Divide Ecosystem in Montana. In the life-simulation video game "The Sims," players give virtual humans personality traits, preferences and needs, and then drop them into a virtual environment to see how they behave.
Sells built the model using the GPS collaring data from 65 grizzly bears navigating individual paths through greenery, riparian areas and around forests and roads. Then, she "parachutes" an individual digital bear into a detailed computer simulation of real-world terrain and has them take thousands of virtual steps. By running these multiple simulated bears through thousands of iterations across the digital terrain, the researchers can watch where the virtual bears repeatedly choose to walk, effectively creating a map of predicted movement corridors.
Sells has used the model to predict how grizzly bears might recolonize the Bitterroot ecosystem of Idaho and Montana, which Lingenpolter was heading toward when attempting to cross Interstate 90.
To get to the Bitterroot Mountains, bears must pass through a valley filled with people, roads, garbage and fruit trees. "So knowing where they are more likely to end up is helpful to address things that could be difficult for humans or bears," Sells told Live Science.
The people problem
The data is also confirming that the greatest barrier bears face comes from human contact or transportation infrastructure across the entire Yellowstone-to-Yukon region. Studies from across west-central North America report that humans directly or indirectly caused between 77% and 90% of grizzly bear deaths from 1989 to 2015. Hunting, managed kills in urban areas and road and rail collisions all take a toll.
Bears in the wild usually avoid people, but some bears seek out human-dominated areas because they know these places are a source of food. People move to the Elk Valley in southeastern British Columbia because they love nature, but then they plant apple trees in their backyard, which attract bears, said Clayton Lamb, a wildlife scientist at the nonprofit Biodiversity Pathways.
Quickly, a bear eating backyard apples gets labeled a "problem bear," "when really it is a 'people problem,'" Lamb told Live Science.
Even human recreation takes a toll on bears' health and ability to move freely. Lamb's research has shown that grizzly bears try to avoid areas next to busy cycling and hiking trails.
To minimize human-bear conflict, Michelle McLellan, a wildlife ecologist at Biodiversity Pathways, has tracked trail use by both people and grizzlies in the West Kootenay region of British Columbia. McLellan documented people's habits using trail cameras and apps such as Strava Metro. Her research shows that the bears use the trails to move quickly between foraging spots but have learned not to use the trails that are most popular with humans. Consequently, the Nelson Cycling Club decided to close certain trails in the spring and cautioned riders about when and how to use the open trails. "Ride aware, make noise, slow down when needed," the club cautioned in its May newsletter.
Working with information from McLellan, the club has cut back overgrown vegetation along sight lines to prevent mountain bikers from startling bears at close range. They've also constructed wooden platforms on sections of trails that clatter and rumble as bikes pass over them, giving bears early notice of approaching riders. "The key is to not surprise them by making a lot of noise." McLellan told Live Science, noting that grizzlies are more likely to attack if they are surprised.
One advantage of having human mountain biking and hiking trails concentrated close to towns is that it focuses recreation into specific areas, Lamb said. Keeping trails condensed supplies multiple accessible paths and reduces humans encroaching on true wilderness — prime bear habitat. "The goal would be to ensure that there's sufficient recreation opportunities for people to stay healthy and connected to their local landscape while ensuring that wildlife can still move around and access their habitats," Lamb said
Learning to share
As humans increasingly live, work and play in bear territory, it's important to recognize the impact on the animals, Servheen said. "The bears never get a day off," he said. "Every day, they're trying to stay away from people and make a living in a place with multiple people on the landscape."
Bears expend a lot of much-needed energy trying to avoid people, and they won't be able to do that forever, Servheen said. As humans increase the development of private lands and recreation in bear territory, the squeeze is on. "There's going to be more conflicts with bears, and more dead bears," Servheen said.
The bears have done their part, Lamb said. His research has shown that bears living near humans are adapting by becoming mostly nocturnal, which reduces their odds of clashing with humans. "So, we need to meet them where they are at and see what we can do to share the space," Lamb said.
On the human side, people need to make it less tempting for bears to be in human dominated areas, McLellan said. That means keeping garbage stowed and making sure there is no ripe fruit available. "If you live rurally, you want them to be able to pass through your property but not linger near your home or in your front yard," McLellan said.
Bears have proved to be adaptable and persistent; Lingenpolter tried to cross the highway dozens of times before finding a way under. However, Servheen warned that we are putting them in a tough spot. To keep bear populations stable, scientists need data on bear behavior to help inform land management policies that create safe pathways for grizzlies to move through human dominated areas and regulate recreation with bears in mind, Servheen said.
"If we want to have bears in the future, we need to think about the needs bears have for some level of space on the landscape," Servheen said.
Securing that space across the vast Yellowstone to Yukon landscape requires more than just land acquisitions and highway overpasses — it requires increasing public awareness and counteracting the perception that bears are inherently aggressive and irrational, Proctor said. If people understand bear behavior, they can learn to act in ways that neither attract bears nor threaten them. And understanding the totality of bears’ strong drive to survive, and protect each other, can elicit empathy and motivation to protect this iconic species.
- 'It's nature calling to humans, and humans deciding whether or not to reply': Why we need to start paying attention to our mutually beneficial relationships with other species
- Bear hair and fish weirs: Meet the Indigenous people combining modern science with ancestral principles to protect the land
- Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
Early in his career, Proctor captured, immobilized and radio-collared a mother grizzly with her two yearlings, or newly adolescent bears. While the research team worked, the young bears circled quietly at a distance. When the scientists finally stepped back and the mother began to stir, the yearlings approached cautiously. As the mother's groggy head rested on a log, the yearlings' long-clawed front paws delicately explored the radio collar. Then, each one rested its head directly on hers, to form a quiet pile of three bear heads.
"They just wanted to touch mom after this ordeal," Proctor said. "Yes, grizzlies can be rough and dangerous but they can also be gentle at times," Proctor said.
Reporting and travel for this story was supported by the Sitka Foundation and the Science Media Centre of Canada.

Jane Palmer is a Colorado-based journalist who is contributing to Live Science with a focus on biodiversity conservation, neuroscience and mental health. She has written about science for many outlets including Nature, Science, Eos Magazine, Al Jazeera, BBC Earth, BBC Future, Mosaic Science and Proto Magazine. Before becoming a journalist, Palmer was a scientist, and she earned a bachelor's degree in cognitive science and a doctorate in computational molecular modeling from the University of Sheffield in England. She enjoys reading and being outside in nature whenever possible, preferably climbing rocks.

articles.title: Loại quả có vị ngọt nhưng lại tốt cho bệnh nhân tiểu đường, giá nửa triệu/kg vẫn đắt hàng
articles.text:
Vì mang vị ngọt tự nhiên nên loại quả này có thể được sử dụng trong một số thức uống giải khát như trà sâm bổ lượng, trà bí đao, nước la hán nha đam...
Tờ Natural Foodseries cho biết, có một thứ quả được mệnh danh là "trái trường thọ", vỏ cứng, màu nâu nhạt, đó là quả la hán. Sở dĩ nó được gọi như vậy là bởi có chứa nhiều chất chống oxy hóa, giúp cơ thể phòng ngừa được rất nhiều rủi ro về sức khỏe.
GS Đỗ Tất Lợi đã viết trong cuốn sách "Những cây thuốc và vị thuốc Việt Nam" về loại quả này như sau: Quả la hán có nguồn gốc từ Trung Quốc, được sử dụng trong một số bài thuốc để trị long đờm, ho, khó chịu ở cổ họng. Vì mang vị ngọt tự nhiên nên loại quả này có thể được sử dụng trong một số thức uống giải khát như trà sâm bổ lượng, trà bí đao, nước la hán nha đam...
Giá một cân la hán khô dao động từ 300-500 ngàn đồng/kg.
Quả la hán được bán rất rộng rãi ở các cửa hàng đồ khô, hoặc các hiệu thuốc, phòng khám Đông y trên cả nước. Giá một cân la hán khô dao động từ 300-500 ngàn đồng/kg, tuy giá thành không rẻ nhưng vì có lợi cho sức khỏe nên được rất nhiều người tìm mua.
Quả la hán là loại quả siêu ngọt, theo Cơ quan Quản lý Dược phẩm và Thực phẩm Hoa Kỳ (FDA), chất tạo ngọt trong quả la hán có tên là mogroside, có vị ngọt gấp 100-250 đường trắng. Đáng nói, dù có vị ngọt nhưng mogroside lại không có giá trị dinh dưỡng, không chứa calo, cũng không làm tăng đường huyết. Do đó nó được xem là có lợi cho bệnh nhân tiểu đường. Với người đang giảm cân, mỡ máu cao... cũng có thể sử dụng loại quả này thay thế cho đường.
Trang Naturalnews thậm chí còn nhận xét quả la hán là thực phẩm thay thế đường lành mạnh. Bạn có thể sử dụng nó trong việc pha trà, cà phê, smoothie, sữa chua, bột yến mạch, hoặc món tráng miệng lành mạnh... thay đường và các chất tạo ngọt khác.
La hán là loại quả vị ngọt, tính mát, không độc.
Theo lương y Võ Thuận Hóa (Phó Chủ tịch Hội Đông Y tỉnh Đắk Lắk): La hán là loại quả vị ngọt, tính mát, không độc. Có khả năng tăng cường hệ miễn dịch, chống dị ứng, trị viêm hầu họng, khản tiếng, táo bón...
